title: Tariffs increased in 2025; why did U.S. imports grow?
abstract: The U.S. average tariff rate increased from 2.9 percent in January 2025 to 14.8 percent in December, a rise of almost 12 percentage points. The surge—the largest such U.S. jump since the Smoot-Hawley tariffs at the onset of the Great Depression in 1930—led to a sharp increase in the tariff-inclusive prices that U.S. importers paid.

title: Too Little too Late? Nationwide Carbon Trading in China
abstract: China launched a nationwide, rate-based carbon market in 2021.Covering the world's top CO2 emitter, compliance depends on the intensity of carbon emissions rather than an absolute cap.We draw on the theoretical literature of rate-based systems to provide the first empirical evidence on an early adopter.Using plant-level data from satellite imagery and machine learning methods, we find that high-efficiency power plants increased electricity generation and CO2 emissions by approximately 5% relative to low-efficiency plants.Because its carbon market regulates nearly all coal plants in China, we focus on the differential responses by plant efficiency, finding no evidence of a differential reduction in emission intensity (though these estimates are imprecise).Relative to coal plants in Indonesia and the Philippines, which had no carbon market, China's high-efficiency plants also increased emissions, while the estimate for its low-efficiency plants is small and insignificant.This pattern of responses suggests that emissions increases of highefficiency plants exceeded substitution away from low-efficiency plants.Underscoring the production stimulus to more efficient Chinese plants, air quality worsened downwind of highefficiency plants relative to low-efficiency plants, compromising air quality in relatively clean areas of China.If China's goal is to reduce its carbon emissions, then benchmarks will need to be tightened within the existing system or an alternative system that does not simultaneously incentivize electricity production will need to be adopted.

title: Artificial intelligence and climate change: balancing innovation and sustainability
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming an increasingly important factor in the climate transition. AI can improve energy efficiency, optimise resource use, accelerate climate innovation and strengthen climate forecasting, adaptation and risk management. At the same time, the development and deployment of AI require substantial computational resources, increasing electricity demand and, depending on the carbon intensity and timing of electricity use, associated emissions.

title: Living in a Ghost Town: The Geography of Depopulation and Aging
abstract: How do depopulation and population aging evolve differently across regions within a country, and what are their implications for aggregate economic activity and regional inequality?Using spatially disaggregated data from Japan over the past several decades, we show that rural areas have experienced significantly faster depopulation and aging than urban areas, driven by low fertility and sustained out-migration of young cohorts.Regions undergoing these trends face declining local amenities and rising per-capita public service costs.To study the future evolution and economic consequences of these dynamics, we develop and calibrate a dynamic life-cycle spatial general equilibrium model.The model predicts widening geographic disparities in depopulation, aging, and economic activity in the coming centuries.While subsidies to declining regions can lower regional inequality, they come at the cost of lower aggregate efficiency and higher public service expenditures.

title: Macroeconomic Effects of Forced Displacement in Sub-Saharan Africa
abstract: This paper estimates the macroeconomic effects of forced displacement on host economies in SubSaharan Africa, drawing on cross-country panel data and country case studies of Burkina Faso, South Sudan, and Uganda to provide granular evidence on the consequences of spatial concentrations of forcibly displaced persons within countries. Estimates from a difference-in-differences local projections (LP-DiD) framework do not suggest that large refugee inflows significantly affect host-country GDP, inflation, or the current account balance over a five-year horizon. The effects on the primary fiscal balance also appear to be muted, yet this masks offsetting fiscal dynamics: government expenditures rise and fiscal revenues increase (mainly through taxes). These results are robust to restricting the control group to Sub-Saharan African economies. Under a broader treatment definition that captures the total displaced population (refugees and internally displaced persons), the GDP response turns significantly negative and intensifies with displacement severity, though this estimate is best interpreted as an upper bound because it cannot be fully separated from the effects of conflict itself that generates displacement. The cross-country findings are consistent with the case studies, which indicate generally muted effects on aggregate food inflation and wages. Beneath this muted aggregate response, however, a consistent pattern emerges across cases: prices of imported and processed staples rise, while those of locally produced cereals stay flat or fall. The case studies also yield mixed evidence regarding the impacts of displacement inflows on consumption and labor force participation, with such inflows reducing host employment in Burkina Faso but raising it in Uganda.

title: Stablecoin-on-Creditor Violence
abstract: The GENIUS Act of 2025 rewrites the priority and estate-property rules that govern the failure of a payment stablecoin issuer. It removes an issuer's required reserves from the bankruptcy estate and grants stablecoin holders a superpriority, capped at any reserve shortfall, over what remains. The commentary so far asks what happens inside bankruptcy once an issuer files—whether holders are actually paid and whether the case can be administered. This article identifies a different problem that arises before a filing. Because reserve assets leave the estate the moment they back a coin, a distressed firm can issue stablecoins to subordinate its existing creditors, hollow out the value a future administrator would need, and, when the firm is a bank, shift losses onto the deposit insurer and potentially the taxpayer. We call this stablecoin-on-creditor violence, drawing an analogy with the phenomenon of creditor-on-creditor violence that began with the 2016 J. Crew dropdown. Unlike in that episode, the stablecoin dropdown is on a statutory footing, meaning it is largely beyond the reach of the doctrines courts use to police its private-law cousins. We show that the subordination is accomplished by the rule carrying reserves out of the estate rather than by the celebrated superpriority. We raise concerns for financial stability: The threat of a dropdown grows with a firm's holdings of safe assets, meaning that creditors may respond negatively to a firm with a more liquid balance sheet. The harm is gravest when the subordinated creditor is the FDIC or another deposit insurer, because losses can be imposed on the rest of the financial system and the taxpayer. Importantly, the problems we raise do not rely on there being any investor demand for stablecoins. We close with a menu of responses and recommend a layered fix that federal regulators could largely implement on their own.

title: Convenience Yields, Risk Premiums, and the Interpretation of Oil Futures Prices During Times of Geopolitical Conflict
abstract: Erik Heitfield , Yang-Ho Park and Erfan Danesh Earlier this year the Middle East conflict led to one of the largest global oil supply shocks in history (Bordoff and O'Sullivan, 2026). Past empirical research has found that commodity futures prices provide accurate predictions of future spot prices under normal market conditions (Reeve and Vigfusson, 2011; Chernenko et al., 2004).

title: US monetary policy spillovers through global commercial real estate
abstract: We provide new evidence on the international spillover effects of US monetary policy through global commercial real estate (CRE) markets. Using a global VAR-X model that exploits both city- and country-level data, we account for spatial dependencies arising from cross-border investor ownership of CRE. A US quantitative easing shock leads to a persistent rise in CRE prices, both within and outside the US, and an expansion of credit, but mostly in the US. To interpret these findings, we develop an open economy New Keynesian model with CRE markets, which highlights the role of increased domestic demand for foreign CRE as a key transmission channel. Moreover, the model reveals that spillover effects can spill back to the US via trade linkages, amplifying the initial effects of US monetary policy.

title: Corporate Sector Stress Testing with Endogenous Balance Sheet Dynamics
abstract: This paper presents a stress test framework for nonfinancial corporate (NFC) balance sheets. The model simulates firm income statements and balance sheets conditional on macro-financial scenarios, to obtain conventional risk metrics such as probabilities of default (PDs) and loss given default (LGD), alongside other structural metrics such as interest coverage ratios, leverage, and others. The model entails explicit stock–flow accounting and a link of borrowing costs to firm-specific credit risk metrics, i.e., an endogenous cost of funding feedback. An illustration is provided with an application to Brazil, involving 8,000 private firms and three hundred listed nonfinancial firms. The results point to heightened vulnerabilities under stagflation shock scenarios, which jointly weaken earnings and raise funding costs, increasing default risk and debt at risk.

source: Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City
title: A Brief History of Deposit Tokens and Tokenized Deposits
abstract: The tokenization of commercial bank deposits has been in development globally since the late 2010s, evolving from theory and experimentation to the more recent implementation of both deposit tokens and tokenized deposits. Tokenizing commercial bank deposits has implications for other blockchain-based payment instruments, such as stablecoins, as well as for legacy payments systems, presenting banks with new opportunities and challenges.

title: Firm Adaptation in Production Networks: Evidence from Extreme Weather Events in Pakistan
abstract: This paper considers how far private adaptation may reduce future vulnerability to climate risks. Using data on monthly firm-to-firm transactions from Pakistan, we find that flood-affected firms are more likely to relocate to safer ground and shift purchases toward suppliers in less flood-prone regions and reached via less flood-prone roads. The results indicate that firms are imperfectly informed about flood risk and update their beliefs following floods. We quantify aggregate impacts using a spatial model of endogenous production network formation. The findings suggest that firms' learning will shape the economic impact of increasingly frequent climate-related disasters. (JEL D22, L14, O13, O14, Q54, R32)

title: Taxing Top Wealth: Migration Responses and Their Aggregate Economic Implications
abstract: Using administrative data from Scandinavian countries, we provide evidence on international migration responses to wealth taxes and evaluate their aggregate economic implications. We find significant migration responses among the wealthy: A 1 percentage point increase in the top wealth tax rate decreases the stock of wealthy taxpayers by about 2 percent. A large fraction of the wealthy are business owners, and their businesses are negatively affected by owner out-migration. The aggregate effects are nevertheless modest: The migration responses to a 1 percentage point increase in the top wealth tax rate reduce employment by 0.02 percent, investments by 0.07 percent, and value added by 0.10 percent. (JEL D31, E22, E24, F22, H24, L26, K34)

title: Industrial Policy via the IPO Market
abstract: This paper studies how China uses access to public equity markets as an instrument of industrial policy.We find that policy-favored status, rather than industry Tobin's Q, predicts IPO activity, in contrast to the United States.The effect is economically large: our estimates imply that favored industries had 287% more IPOs and 148% higher IPO proceeds than non-favored industries over 2002 to 2022.We develop a framework to interpret these findings: the government shapes the number of listing opportunities available across industries, while market forces determine which firms obtain these opportunities based on firm fundamentals.Consistent with our framework, policy favor also predicts a valuation premium which persists after listing.

title: Fiscal integration as a Pareto improvement
abstract: Fiscal integration in a currency union is generally understood as a transfer from fiscally strong to fiscally weak countries. I show that this changes when common debt is paired with a non-defaultable common tax, even if national debt remains defaultable. The risky country gains from intertemporal trade: it receives a grant financed by a perpetual obligation it discounts more heavily than lenders do. The cost to the safe member is second-order and the tax removes it by insuring imperfectly correlated cycles rather than transferring resources in expectation. The calibration delivers a narrow Pareto-improving region: the tax that eliminates the risky country’s perverse incentive to default is negligible, while the tax that compensates the safe country is an order of magnitude larger. Joint spending on a public good expands the region and reverses that ordering: the safe country gains even before the common budget balances.

title: Price Gouging and the Monopoly Option
abstract: We investigate a dynamic oligopoly model with two phases: a normal phase where an essential input is available, and a disruption phase where firms must rely on inventories. Disruptions create an overcutting pricing incentive arising from the option to forgo sales and monopolize the market once rivals stock out. This monopoly option causes the price to jump to a supracompetitive level at the advent of the disruption and to remain above the competitive price path throughout. Price caps raise welfare, but reduce inventory investment. Government reserves reduce prices and raise buffer stocks, as do reserve mandates when financially feasible.

title: Climate Risk and Sustainable Finance: Bridging Policy, Research and Practice
abstract: The challenges that climate change poses to the financial system require bringing together the knowledge and experience of central banks, policymakers, academics and experts. In this context, on 25 March 2026, the Banco de España organised the conference “Climate Risk and Sustainable Finance: Bridging Policy, Research and Practice”, together with the Network for Greening the Financial System, the Centre for Economic Transition Expertise and the Transition Pathway Initiative Centre at the London School of Economics. The main contributions are presented in this joint publication by the Banco de España and the journal Papeles de Energía published by Funcas.

title: Union Bargaining Power and the Amenity-Wage Trade-Off
abstract: This paper studies how collective bargaining affects wages and amenities. By merging collective bargaining agreements (CBAs) to linked employer-employee data in Brazil, I combine rich contracted amenities with wage information. I implement a difference-in-differences strategy that exploits a court ruling enforcing CBA continuation (i.e., ultra-activity) to estimate the effects of union bargaining power. Strengthening unions raises wages and amenities without reducing employment—increasing retention despite some labor-labor substitution. A revealed-preference approach shows that amenities account for 45 percent of total compensation gains. These findings suggest that collective bargaining can offset monopsony power, but employers retain the right-to-manage workforce composition. (JEL J31, J32, J42, J51, J52, O15)

source: Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco
title: The Impacts of Unauthorized Immigration on U.S. Labor and Housing Markets: New Evidence from Administrative Microdata
abstract: From early 2021 through early 2024, the U.S. experienced an unprecedented boom in unauthorized immigration, with substantial heterogeneity across local economies. Using administrative microdata, we construct new measures of national and local unauthorized immigration flows and exploit exogenous variation using multiple empirical designs. Unauthorized immigrant worker flows increased local employment approximately one-for-one, with mixed evidence of wage depression. They also raised house prices and rents without expanding housing supply. Finally, these flows reduced labor income per capita and government transfers. These findings help inform debates surrounding how unauthorized immigration impacts labor and housing markets and public finances in the U.S.

source: Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City
title: Beyond Valuations: Long-Term Financial Risks from the AI Build-Out
abstract: Large-scale investments associated with the artificial intelligence (AI) build-out have encompassed a broad range of industries, financial institutions, and markets, generating investor exuberance but also concerns about the disorderly repricing of assets. The financial risks associated with AI investment extend beyond short-term valuation distortions and may entail significant long-term structural shifts.

title: What volatility reveals: Agnostic identification of exchange rate and treasury-market dynamics in inconvenient times
abstract: Why did the US dollar depreciate and long-term US Treasury yields rise after the April 2025 U.S. tariff announcements even though markets clearly moved into “risk-off” mode? We address this puzzle using high-frequency asset price data and a flexible econometric approach that exploits changes in volatility to let the data themselves speak about the mechanisms at work. Our findings show that the episode cannot be understood as the effect of a single tariff shock. Rather, it reflects the interaction of safe-haven demand, confidence in U.S. institutions, Treasury-market intermediation, and changes in the convenience value of dollar-denominated safe assets. This combination helps explain why the dollar weakened in spite of an initial flight to safety. A tariff shock unlike previous tariff shocks We study the financial market impact of the US tariff announcement made on 2 April 2025. The US Administration imposed tariffs on almost all trading partners, including a 10 % baseline tariff on imports from 180 countries and an additional “reciprocal” component linked to bilateral trade imbalances. On the day of the announcement, markets behaved as we would expect in a global risk-off episode: equity prices fell, volatility spiked, and investors sought safety. However, in the days that followed, two features stood out: the US dollar depreciated against the euro, while long-term US Treasury yields rose. This pattern is at odds with both standard safe haven behavior and canonical open economy trade theory. In typical global risk episodes, higher risk premia result in a stronger dollar and lower US yields as investors rush into dollar-denominated safe assets. Furthermore, in dominant currency models of trade, tariffs imposed by a country like the United States tend to appreciate its currency via expenditure switching. Earlier US tariff episodes, such as the 2018‑2019 trade war, fit these predictions: they were associated with dollar appreciation and compressed term spreads. The 2025 episode, however, did not. We therefore question whether the April 2025 market reaction can be explained by a single “tariff shock,” or whether it reflects the interaction of multiple, distinct financial shocks. Two key shocks: safe haven and U.S. Institutional Credibility The heteroskedastic VAR model statistically identifies a set of structural shocks. We focus on the two that are most relevant for the “Liberation Day” episode. The first is a safe haven shock that captures a conventional global risk-off event. In response to such a shock, equity prices fall together with yields on long-term US Treasury yields. At the same time, the dollar appreciates against the euro as demand increases for US safe assets in response to a rise in market volatility. The second shock has a very different dynamic pattern and is crucial for understanding the post-announcement dynamics. US long-term Treasury yields rise and the exchange rate depreciates against the euro . We interpret this as a deterioration in confidence in the institutional and policy environment underpinning the international role of the United States and label it as a US Institutional Credibility shock. How these shocks explain the “Liberation Day” and why 2019 was different We use historical decompositions to quantify how much each shock contributed to the observed movements in asset prices around April 2025 and, for comparison, around the August 2019 tariff escalation. In the case of the April 2025 event, we find that the safe haven shock explains most of the fall in equity prices and the spike in volatility. The episode initially looks like a standard global risk-off event. In the subsequent days, the unusual combination of a weaker dollar and higher long-term US yields are driven primarily by the US Institutional Credibility shock. This shock becomes dominant after the initial market reaction, accounting for the persistent depreciation of the dollar and the widening of the US term spread. In the case of the August 2019 tariff escalation, by contrast, we find that this episode is largely explained by shocks with a safe haven profile and that the US Institutional Credibility shock plays a minor role. Term spreads compress and the dollar behaves in the same way as during a typical safe haven episode, in line with earlier findings on trade war episodes. This comparison shows that April 2025 was not just a “bigger 2019.” Rather, it activated an additional mechanism: a rise in Treasury risk premia that weakened the dollar and raised long-term yields, on top of the initial risk-off response. Ter Steege, L., S. Velasco (2026), What volatility reveals: Agnostic identification of exchange rate and treasury-market dynamics in inconvenient times, Bundesbank Discussion Paper, No 34/2026

title: A Global DSGE Model for Oil-Dependent Economies
abstract: This paper develops a global DSGE model linking oil-dependent economies to the systemic economies, and applies it to the GCC countries. The model features a range of nominal and real rigidities, extensive macrofinancial linkages, and diverse spillover transmission channels. Its modular structure also encompasses common features of oil-dependent economies, including a state-owned oil company, a capital intensive oil extraction technology, a sovereign wealth fund, an oil consumption subsidy, and membership of an international oil cartel. The calibrated model is used to simulate global risk and domestic reform scenarios the GCC economies, revealing how their distinct structural characteristics shape their responses to shocks.

title: Moving Out: Geoeconomic Policy and the Relocation of Foreign Affiliates
abstract: Governments increasingly use trade and industrial policy to reshape where multinationals produce, yet standard measures of this geoeconomic pressure are aggregate and cannot detect origin-specific discrimination. We build a bilateral, directional index of relative protectionism that measures how restrictive a destination is toward a given origin. We combine it with bilateral geopolitical risk indices and global ownership links over the period 2010-21, and estimate a gravity-type Poisson-Pseudo Maximum Likelihood model with three-way fixed effects. Our results show that where bilateral protectionism is greater, foreign-affiliate presence is markedly smaller: a 1 percentage point increase in the index is associated with 1.3% fewer subsidiaries than that origin-destination pair would otherwise have. The main mechanism runs through an operational hostility channel (e.g. discriminatory subsidies, procurement exclusion), which outweighs an offsetting tariff-jumping channel and concentrates in non-tradable sectors, where serving the market requires local presence. The estimates show no evidence of anticipation and are robust to longer lags and sample splits. Bilateral geopolitical risk enters with the same negative sign, adding a smaller but complementary layer of fragmentation risk to the effect of geoeconomic policy.

title: Headwind or tailwind? How banks interpret borrowers’ AI exposure
abstract: General-purpose technologies create large opportunities but make their distribution across firms difficult to assess in real time. We use banks as interpreters of the rise of generative AI by studying lender-specific probability-of-default (PD) estimates for private firms in four large euro-area economies. As public attention to AI rises after ChatGPT, banks lower assessed default risk for borrowers in highly AI-exposed industries by about 5%. The reassessment is weaker for labor-intensive firms and stronger among lenders with pre-existing industry expertise. Yet the favorable industry-level effect is accompanied by a systematic reordering within product markets: banks reassess firms with stronger pre-ChatGPT market positions less favorably relative to their competitors, compressing the risk advantage associated with market leadership. Credit allocation moves in the same direction, with market leaders experiencing relatively lower drawn and committed credit, more relationship exits, and fewer new lenders. The reordering also predicts subsequent bad-credit events beyond banks’ consensus PDs. Internal bank assessments therefore provide a forward-looking measure of how generative AI is expected to reshape competitive risk.

title: Superbonus and work injuries in the construction sector in Italy
abstract: The Superbonus led to a rapid and substantial increase in economic activity in Italy's construction sector. Periods of expansion of this kind typically entail an increase in workplace injury rates. This paper examines whether the rise in construction employment induced by the Superbonus was accompanied by a change in the construction injury rate. Between 2021 and 2023, the Superbonus led to an increase in construction employment and, contrary to expectations, a decline in the rate of severe workplace injuries. The effect was stronger in the regions where the incentive was used more extensively. It is plausible that firms strengthened preventive measures, since violations of workplace safety regulations could have resulted in the loss of this substantial incentive.

source: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
title: From Moore’s Law to Eroom’s Law: Power Constraints and the Productivity Slowdown
abstract: Economic growth depends on combining existing inputs into new inventions. However, these combinations are not always physically feasible. One important example is dark silicon, where power and cooling limits prevent all the transistors on a chip from operating at once. I develop a growth model motivated by these limitations and establish conditions for a unique balanced growth path where electronic miniaturization and power efficiency grow at the same rate. When power-efficiency research becomes harder, both total research employment and productivity growth fall on the new balanced growth path. With gradual adjustment of research employment, I construct a local equilibrium transition in which more researchers temporarily coexist with slower productivity growth. This Eroom’s law result holds for small shocks in a two-dimensional design space with sufficiently similar industry constraints.
